Review: Units 10–14

Unit 10.1

Talking about jobs

Use a form of to be (am, is, are) with a or an and a job title to say what someone does. Use a before a job that starts with a consonant sound, and an before a job that starts with a vowel sound. Plural jobs do not use a or an.

I am a police officer. He is an engineer. She is a nurse. They are teachers. We are artists.

Choosing a or an

First soundArticleExample
Consonant soundaa teacher
Vowel soundanan engineer
Plural jobno articleteachers

Say the job title out loud to check the sound, not just the first letter — "an hour" starts with a vowel sound even though "hour" begins with the letter H.

Grammar practice: complete each sentence

  1. (I) I a taxi driver.
  2. (he) He an actor.
  3. (they) They firefighters.
  4. a job that starts with a vowel sound She is engineer.
  5. a job that starts with a consonant sound He is chef.
  6. (we) We doctors.
  7. asking about someone's job you a teacher?
  8. plural jobs need no article My parents accountants.

Reading practice

At the job fair, everyone talks about their work. Amara says, "I am a nurse at the city hospital." Next to her, a tall man smiles. "I'm Tomas. I am an electrician." Two students walk by with name tags. "We are volunteers today," they say. A woman in a red jacket introduces her husband. "This is my husband. He is a firefighter." Later, a group of teenagers stops at a table about computers. "Are you a programmer?" one asks the man at the table. "Yes," he says, "I am a programmer for a small company." By the end of the day, everyone knows a little more about the jobs at the fair.

Check your understanding

1. Amara is a nurse.

2. Tomas is a firefighter.

3. The two students are volunteers.

4. The woman's husband is a firefighter.

5. The man at the computer table says he is not a programmer.

Units 10.8, 10.11

Using "work in," "work on," and "work with"

Use work in for a place or building, like an office or a hospital. Use work on for a specific site or project, like a farm, a ship, or a film set. Use work with for people, animals, or things you work alongside.

I work in a hospital. I work on a farm. I work with animals. She works in an office downtown. He works with computers all day.

work in / on / with

PhraseUsed forExample
work ina building or placework in a school
work ona specific site or projectwork on a farm
work withpeople, animals, or thingswork with children

A farm, a ship, and a film set are places too, but we use "work on" for these specific kinds of locations, not "work in."

Grammar practice: complete each sentence

  1. a place, a hospital I work a hospital.
  2. a farm My uncle works a farm.
  3. animals She works animals every day.
  4. an office He works a large office.
  5. a ship My cousin works a fishing ship.
  6. children I work young children at the school.
  7. a restaurant They work a small restaurant downtown.
  8. a movie set The actors work a busy film set.

His daughter, Mrs. Kim, works in a busy hospital downtown. She works with patients all day long. Her son, Daniel, works on a fishing boat every summer, but in winter he takes a job at a warehouse instead. Daniel's sister, Yuna, works with computers at a technology company. "I love my job," she says, "but I also love visiting Grandpa's farm on weekends."

Check your understanding

1. Grandpa Kim works on a farm.

2. Mrs. Kim works with animals.

3. Daniel works on a fishing boat in summer.

4. Yuna works with computers.

5. The whole family works at the same hospital.

Units 11.1, 11.2

Telling the time

Use It's with a number to say the hour, or with o'clock for a full hour. Use half past for 30 minutes after the hour, and quarter past or quarter to for 15 minutes before or after. Ask the time with What time is it?

It's five. It's five o'clock. It's half past three. It's quarter to nine. What time is it?

Saying the time

TimeHow to say it
3:00It's three o'clock.
3:15It's quarter past three.
3:30It's half past three.
3:45It's quarter to four.

We can say "It's three" or "It's three o'clock" for an exact hour — both are correct.

Grammar practice: complete each sentence

  1. 7:00 It's seven .
  2. 2:30 It's past two.
  3. 9:15 It's past nine.
  4. 5:45 It's quarter six.
  5. asking for the time time is it?
  6. 12:00 It's twelve .
  7. 4:30 It's past four.
  8. 10:15 It's quarter ten.

Reading practice

Mia checks her watch. "What time is it?" she asks her brother. "It's quarter past eight," he says. "Our bus leaves at eight thirty!" They hurry to the bus stop. By the time they arrive, it's half past eight, and the bus is just pulling away. At school, the first class starts at nine o'clock. During lunch, Mia looks at the clock again. "It's quarter to twelve," she tells her friend. "We have fifteen more minutes." After school, Mia's mother picks her up. "It's five o'clock already," her mother says. "Time flies!"

Check your understanding

1. The bus leaves at eight thirty.

2. Mia and her brother catch the bus easily.

3. The first class starts at nine o'clock.

4. Mia has fifteen more minutes at lunch.

5. Mia's mother picks her up at four o'clock.

Show transcript

Man: What time does the train leave tomorrow?

Woman: It leaves at quarter past nine.

Man: OK. So let's meet at the station at half past eight.

Woman: Half past eight is too early. Let's meet at quarter to nine.

Man: Fine. And what time does it arrive in Boston?

Woman: At twelve o'clock.

Man: Great. Lunch at half past twelve, then?

Woman: Perfect. The museum closes at five, so we have lots of time.

Unit 13.1

The present simple

Use the present simple for habits and routines. Add -s to the verb for he, she, and it. Do not add -s for I, you, we, and they.

I eat lunch at noon every day. She eats lunch at 2pm every day. We walk to school together. He walks to work every morning. They drink coffee every morning.

Verb form in the present simple

SubjectVerb formExample
I / You / We / Theybase formeat, walk, drink
He / She / Itbase + -seats, walks, drinks

Some verbs need -es instead of just -s, like goes, watches, and does.

Grammar practice: choose the correct verb form

  1. (I / eat) I breakfast at seven.
  2. (she / eat) She lunch at noon.
  3. (he / walk) He to school every day.
  4. (they / drink) They tea in the morning.
  5. (it / open) The store at nine.
  6. (we / watch) We a movie every Friday.
  7. (he / go) My brother to the gym twice a week.
  8. (she / finish) She work at five.

Reading practice

Every day, Noah wakes up early. He eats a big breakfast before work. His sister Zoe drinks tea instead of coffee. At the bakery, Zoe bakes bread every morning before it opens. Noah drives to his office and starts work at eight. In the evening, the whole family cooks dinner together, and Noah's father washes the dishes. On weekends, they relax at home and watch movies together.

Check your understanding

1. Noah eats a big breakfast.

2. Zoe drinks coffee every morning.

3. Zoe bakes bread before the bakery opens.

4. Noah starts work at eight.

5. Noah's father cooks dinner alone every night.

My name is Owen, and I'm a baker. I get up at four o'clock every morning. I drink a coffee and walk to the bakery. I start work at half past four. I make bread, cakes, and cookies. My wife works at the bakery, too. She opens the shop at seven and sells our bread to the customers. I finish work at one o'clock. In the afternoon, I sleep for two hours. Unit 14.2

Prepositions and days of the week

Use on before a specific day of the week, like on Monday. Use from and to together to show a range of days, like from Monday to Friday.

I work on Mondays. I work from Monday to Friday. The store is closed on Sundays. We meet from Tuesday to Thursday. Classes start on Wednesday.

on vs. from...to

PrepositionUseExample
onone specific dayon Monday
from...toa range of daysfrom Monday to Friday

We can say "on Saturdays" (plural, a general habit) or "on Saturday" (this specific day) — both are common.

The days of the week

DayType
MondayWeekday
TuesdayWeekday
WednesdayWeekday
ThursdayWeekday
FridayWeekday
SaturdayWeekend
SundayWeekend

Days of the week always start with a capital letter, even in the middle of a sentence: "I have class on Tuesday and Thursday."

Grammar practice: choose the right preposition

  1. one day I work Mondays.
  2. a range of days, the start The gym is open Monday to Saturday.
  3. a range of days, the end The gym is open from Monday Saturday.
  4. one day The store is closed Sundays.
  5. a range of days Classes meet Tuesday to Thursday.
  6. one day We have a test Friday.
  7. a range of days The office is open Monday to Friday.
  8. one day Her birthday party is Saturday.

Reading practice

From Tuesday to Thursday, she sees patients in the afternoon. On Fridays, she leaves work early to pick up her daughter. The clinic is closed on Sundays, so Priya spends the day with her family. On Saturdays, she usually relaxes at home or goes for a walk.

Check your understanding

1. Priya works from Monday to Friday.

2. The clinic is busiest on Fridays.

3. Priya sees patients in the afternoon from Tuesday to Thursday.

4. The clinic is open on Sundays.

5. Priya relaxes on Saturdays.

Listen to the conversation. You can pause it, replay it, or slow it down. Then decide if each sentence is true or false.

“Joining a gym”

0:00 / 0:46 Speed

Check your understanding

1. The gym is open on Sundays.

2. Yoga is on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

Show transcript

Woman: Hi, I want to join the gym. When are you open?

Man: We're open from Monday to Saturday. On Sundays, we're closed.

Woman: And when are the yoga classes?

Man: Yoga is on Tuesdays and Thursdays, at six in the evening.

Woman: Great. Do you have swimming lessons?

Man: Yes. Swimming lessons are on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays.

Woman: Hmm, I work late on Wednesdays. Is there a class on Saturday?

Man: Yes, there's a swimming class on Saturday mornings, too.

Woman: Perfect. I'll come on Saturdays.

Units 14.8, 14.9

Frequency phrases

Use frequency phrases like once a week, twice a month, or three times a year to say how often something happens. Use every day, every week, or every month for something that happens each time.

I go to the gym twice a week. She visits her parents once a month. We travel three times a year. He calls his brother every day. They clean the house every week.

Saying how often

How oftenPhraseExample
1 timeonce a ___once a week
2 timestwice a ___twice a month
3+ times___ times a ___three times a year
each timeevery ___every day

After two, we say "twice," not "two times," although "two times" is also understood.

Grammar practice: choose the right frequency word

  1. one time a week I go swimming a week.
  2. two times a month She visits the dentist a month.
  3. three times a year We travel a year.
  4. happens each day He calls his mom day.
  5. one time a year They have a big meeting a year.
  6. happens each week The team practices week.
  7. two times a week I clean my apartment a week.
  8. three times a month She goes to yoga class a month.

Reading practice

Leo has a busy schedule. He goes to the gym twice a week to stay healthy. Once a month, he visits his grandparents in the countryside. His book club meets three times a year for special events, but Leo reads every day on his own. His sister Maya calls their parents every week, even when she is traveling. "I try to see my family once a month," Leo says, "and I never miss my gym days."

Check your understanding

1. Leo goes to the gym twice a week.

2. Leo visits his grandparents every week.

3. The book club meets three times a year.

4. Leo reads every day.

5. Maya calls their parents once a year.

Units 10–14

Speaking practice

Practice speaking like in a speaking exam such as IELTS. Part 1: answer short questions about you. Part 2: prepare for one minute, then talk about a topic for one to two minutes. Part 3: act out a conversation with a partner. Try first, then open the examples.

Part 1: Interview

Answer each question in one to three sentences. Don't just say "yes" or "no" — add a reason or an extra detail.

Jobs

1. What do you do? Are you a student, or do you work?

Show example answer
I'm a student. I study engineering at the university. In the future, I want to be an engineer like my dad.
Jobs

2. What do the people in your family do?

Show example answer
My mother is a nurse, and my father is an electrician. My brother is a student.
Work in / on / with

3. Where do you work or study? What do you work with?

Show example answer
I work in an office downtown. I work with computers all day, and I work with a great team.
Telling the time

4. What time do you get up on weekdays?

Show example answer
I get up at half past six. I leave home at quarter past seven.
Present simple

5. What does your best friend do every morning?

Show example answer
She walks her dog and drinks a big cup of coffee. Then she takes the bus to work.
Days of the week

6. Which days do you work or study?

Show example answer
I study from Monday to Friday. On Saturdays, I work in a shop. I rest on Sundays.
Frequency

7. How often do you exercise?

Show example answer
I go to the gym twice a week, on Tuesdays and Thursdays. I go running once a week.
Frequency

8. How often do you see your family?

Show example answer
I see my parents every weekend, and I visit my grandparents once a month.

Part 2: Long turn

You have one minute to prepare. You can write some notes. Then talk for one to two minutes.

Describe a person you know who has an interesting job.

You should say:

  • who the person is
  • what his or her job is
  • where he or she works and what he or she works with

and explain why you think the job is interesting.

0:00 Press a button to start
Show example answer
I want to talk about my aunt Laura. She's a vet. She works in an animal hospital in my city, and on weekends she works on a farm. She works with dogs, cats, horses, and cows! She starts work at eight o'clock and finishes at six. She works from Monday to Saturday. Twice a month, she visits a zoo to help the animals there. I think her job is interesting because every day is different. One day she helps a small cat, and the next day she helps a big horse. She loves her job, and she's very good at it.

Part 3: Role-plays

Work with a partner. Student A and Student B read only their own card. Then have the conversation.

Careers day interview

Student A writes for the school website. Student B talks about his or her job (real or imaginary).

Student A

  • Ask about B's job.
  • Ask where B works.
  • Ask what time B starts and finishes work.
  • Ask which days B works.
  • Ask how often B travels for work.

Student B

  • Say what your job is.
  • Say where you work and what you work with.
  • Answer A's questions about times and days.
  • Say one thing you love about your job.
Useful languageWhat do you do?Where do you work?What time do you start?I work from… to…once a month / twice a week
Show example dialogue

A: Hi! Thanks for talking to me. What do you do?

B: I'm a chef.

A: Where do you work?

B: I work in a restaurant downtown. I work with a team of six people.

A: What time do you start work?

B: I start at eleven o'clock and finish at half past ten at night.

A: Wow! Which days do you work?

B: I work from Tuesday to Saturday. The restaurant is closed on Sundays and Mondays.

A: How often do you travel for work?

B: About twice a year. I go to food festivals.

A: What do you love about your job?

B: I love cooking for people. It makes them happy!

Finding a time to meet

Student A and Student B want to study together this week. Use your schedule and find a day and time.

Student A

  • Monday: work 9:00 to 5:00
  • Tuesday: free in the afternoon
  • Wednesday: gym at 6:00 p.m.
  • Thursday: free all day

Student B

  • Monday: free in the evening
  • Tuesday: English class 2:00 to 4:00
  • Wednesday: work 8:00 to 3:00
  • Thursday: free from 3:00 p.m.
Useful languageAre you free on…?What time…?I work from… to…How about… at…?That's perfect!
Show example dialogue

A: Let's study together this week. Are you free on Monday?

B: Yes, in the evening. And you?

A: I work from nine to five, so Monday evening is OK, but I'm tired after work. What about Tuesday afternoon?

B: Sorry, I have English class from two to four on Tuesday.

A: Hmm. Are you free on Thursday?

B: Yes, I'm free from three o'clock.

A: Great. How about Thursday at half past three?

B: That's perfect! See you on Thursday.

Units 10–14

Writing practice

Read the task, plan your ideas, and write your text in the box. The counter shows how many words you have — it turns green when you're in the right range. Use the grammar from these units. When you finish, compare your text with the example.

Task 1: My daily routine

Paragraph50–70 words

Write about a normal weekday in your life.

Write about

  • what time you get up
  • what you do in the morning
  • where you work or study
  • what you do in the evening

Try to use

  • present simple (I get up, she works)
  • telling the time (at half past seven)
  • work in / on / with
0 words
Show example text (63 words)
I get up at half past six every day. I take a shower and eat breakfast. At quarter past seven, I take the bus to work. I'm a receptionist, and I work in a hotel. I work with tourists from many countries. I finish work at four o'clock. In the evening, I cook dinner and watch TV. I go to bed at eleven.

Task 2: My week

Message60–80 words

A friend wants to see you this week. Write a message about your week and say when you're free.

Write about

  • which days you work or study
  • what you do on some days of the week
  • how often you do some activities
  • when you're free to meet

Try to use

  • on Monday / from Monday to Friday
  • once a week / twice a month / every day
  • present simple
0 words
Show example text (65 words)
Hi Sam! I'd love to see you! I work from Monday to Friday, from nine to five. On Tuesdays and Thursdays, I go to the gym after work. I have English class once a week, on Wednesday evening. On Saturday mornings, I play soccer with my friends. I'm free on Friday evening and on Sunday. How about Sunday at two o'clock? See you soon, Lia

Talking about jobs

1. I ____ a nurse.

2. She ____ a teacher.

3. They ____ engineers.

4. Which is correct for a job that starts with a vowel sound?

5. Which sentence uses "a" correctly?

Using "work in," "work on," and "work with"

6. I work ____ a hospital.

7. My uncle works ____ a farm.

8. She works ____ animals.

Telling the time

17. They ____ tea every morning. (drink)

Prepositions and days of the week

23. The gym is open from Monday ____ Saturday.

Frequency phrases
